newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Imran replays anti-corruption message to voters.
newsitem.headline: Imran replays anti-corruption message to voters.

text.p: Imran Khan, Pakistan's former cricket captain, cut a dashing figure on the campaign trail but pollsters say he will make little impact in Monday's election.
As he toured the country, Imran preached his anti-corruption message in simple, direct language, but the crowds were small.

A political novice, Imran portrays himself as a new force that can clean up a system he says has been sullied by former prime ministers Nawaz Sharif and Benazir Bhutto, President Farooq Leghari and Bhutto's husband Asif Ali Zardari.
"Mian (Sharif), Bibi (Bhutto), Zardari and Leghari are all the same," he said at one rally. "They have robbed the country, they have robbed the people. Now let's put a stop to it."
Imran, who formed his Tehrik-i-Insaaf (Justice Movement) only nine months ago, is a candidate in nine constituencies in his bid for a seat in the 217-member National Assembly.
But opinion polls suggest his fledgling party will win few, if any seats, against its well-established opponents.
Imran promises that he will topple a political system that he says robs the poor and enriches the wealthy.
This is a bold ambition in Pakistan, where Bhutto's Pakistan People's Party (PPP) and Sharif's Pakistan Muslim League (PML) have dominated politics since military rule ended in 1988.

Despite popular perceptions that corruption flourished under both leaders, Bhutto and Sharif are front runners in the election called by Leghari after he sacked Bhutto's government on November 5, alleging corruption and misrule.
Leghari pledged that an anti-corruption drive by the caretaker government he named to oversee the elections would clean up the system and bar tainted politicians from the polls.

Yet no important political figures, with the exception of Zardari, who ruled himself out from his jail cell, have been disqualified and the slow progress made by the Ehtesab (Accountability) Commission has disappointed many Pakistanis.
Imran seized on this perceived failure to demand that Leghari resign to ensure free and fair elections.

He alleged that the president had done a secret deal with Sharif, under which the PML leader would be allowed to form the next government on condition that he accepted the advice of a newly-formed Council for Defence and National Security.
Sharif and Leghari, who is chairman of the civilian-military council, have denied cutting any such deal.
Disenchantment with politicians should help Imran, who built a cancer hospital in Lahore after ending his cricket career by leading Pakistan to a 1992 World Cup triumph.

Imran, still lean and athletic at 43, speaks passionately of Pakistan's need for reform. "I can topple these big names, but only with your support, just as I built the cancer hospital with your help," he tells his followers.
Imran's hospital fund-raising campaign, which took him to cities, towns and villages across Pakistan, elicited an enthusiastic response which helped propel him into politics.
Imran, who abandoned his playboy past after rediscovering his Islamic roots, married Jemima Goldsmith, daughter of Anglo-French financier Sir James Goldsmith in 1995.

Imran denies accusations by Nawaz Sharif and Islamic militants that he accepts "Zionist money" from his father-in-law, who is Jewish. The allegations did not seem to be a major factor affecting his campaign.
The wealthy Jemima, a convert to Islam, took a modest part in her husband's political life, attending a few women's meetings and addressing them in hesitant Urdu.

Pakistan's most glamorous couple, who had a son last year, have had to cope with embarrassing allegations from one of Imran's ex-girlfriends, heiress Sita White, that he is the father of her four-year-old daughter Tyrian.
"Sita's accusations have definitely hurt Imran, especially with conservative women voters," said a rueful party worker.
